19697-by-what-authority:
Great Keynes, a quiet backwater village, anchors the opening of By What Authority. A traveler waits there, impatient, while a horse is shod. London's whirl lies twenty miles north of him. The Brighton road rushes eight miles east. Against that stillness, the novel sets its question of authority. The story is a historical romance of England's religious struggles.

The famous tale behind this title concerns a young Catholic in Elizabethan England. Faith and crown pulled subjects in opposite directions then. A village far from court could still feel that pull. The novel uses slow country scenes to build its world. Its question, who may command belief, ran through the age.
20002-alroy-the-prince-of-the-captivity:
Benjamin Disraeli published Alroy in 1833, a romance of the medieval Jewish East. Its hero is David Alroy, the Prince of the Captivity. Disraeli defends his supernatural machinery as Cabalistically correct. From the Spirits of the Tombs to Solomon's sceptre, he claims Hebrew tradition as authority. The novel follows a would-be messiah raising revolt in Persia. Baghdad and the caliph's court frame his rising.

Disraeli, of Jewish descent, made Alroy his one Jewish epic. The historical Alroy led a twelfth-century movement among Kurdish Jews. Disraeli turns him into a Byronic conqueror-poet. Politics, prophecy, and ambition fuse in the hero exactly as in the author. Later prime ministers rarely leave juvenilia this revealing. Alroy is Disraeli dreaming his own destiny eastward.
20032-northern-nut-growers-report-of-the:
Northern nut growers met, spoke, and kept records of their meetings, and one such report survives here. The pages include long lists of members and guests. Names from Washington appear again and again in the roll. Karl W. Greene and T. P. Littlepage are among those listed.

Reports like this one record who came, where they lived, and what the group did. They are plain records, not tales, and their value lies in names and dates. Growers, officials, and keen amateurs all took part in this shared work on nuts and trees.
20160-a-history-of-american-christianity:
Leonard Woolsey Bacon published A History of American Christianity in 1897. Bacon was a minister and church historian of wide learning. He notes how near God's plans came to defeat by human enterprise. Medieval Norse trips to North America now look like fact, he argues.

From those early probes, the book traces churches across the new nation. Colonies, revivals, and new sects all pass in ordered review. Bacon writes as an insider who still weighs proof with care. Readers get a full, dated survey of faith in America to his day.
20174-freedom-truth-and-beauty:
Edward Doyle published Freedom, Truth, and Beauty in 1921, a book of poems and praise. Doyle was known as the blind poet of Harlem in New York. A note urges readers to take up his Haunted Temple poems. There they may feel shame for past moods of distrust and discontent.

His verse turns on faith, sight beyond eyes, and hope in hard life. Blindness shapes his image as a poet who sees by inner light. The book mixes his poems with warm words from his admirers. Readers get a period voice of faith and grit from Harlem's streets.
20337-a-narrative-of-the-mutiny-on-board:
William Bligh wrote A Narrative of the Mutiny on Board His Majesty's Ship Bounty. Bligh sailed from Otaheite on April 4, 1789, with his cargo safe. He carried 1,015 fine bread-fruit plants in the highest state of health. Many other valuable fruits of that country filled the ship too.

Weeks of care had gone into collecting those plants for transport. Weeks later, his crew rose and set him adrift in an open boat. Bligh's own account defends his conduct and tells that famed voyage home. Readers get the captain's voice from history's most famous mutiny.
20606-the-magic-city:
E. Nesbit's The Magic City is a children's fantasy about a boy who builds a city and steps inside it. Philip Haldane and his sister live in a little red-roofed house in a little red-roofed town. They have a little garden, a little balcony, and a little pony in a little stable.

When his sister marries and life changes, Philip builds a great model city from books, toys, and household things. The city becomes real, and Philip must rule and rescue it. Nesbit mixes everyday childhood with true wonder, in the style that made her the founder of modern children's fantasy.
20612-fort-amity:
Arthur Quiller-Couch set his novel Fort Amity in Canada during the French and Indian War. In his preface he hopes his remarks will not seem too pompous for the story he tells. It is a story in which true love is crossed by a soldier's sense of honor.

The theme, he admits, is a variant on a great commonplace. Following his habit, he lets the incidents and the characters make their own impression. Around the frontier fort, war between empires presses on private hearts. Quiller-Couch, who signed himself Q, writes the tale with a poet's care for place and speech.
20708-a-son-of-the-city:
Herman Gastrell Seely's A Son of the City, published in 1917, is a story of boy life in Chicago. Its hero grows up on city streets, with school, gangs, jobs, and baseball for his world. The first chapter's heading promises the pattern: In Which Our Hero Goes Fishing.

The book opens before dawn. Startled from a sound sleep, the boy fumbles beneath the bed to throttle the alarm clock. He must silence its clamor before it wakes the rest of the household. Seely writes city boyhood from the inside, in an age when such everyday stories for boys were rare.
20856-ten-from-infinity:
A Monarch Books science fiction novel from January 1963, Ten From Infinity bears Ivar Jorgensen's name. Ralph Brillhart painted its cover for the paperback trade. The imprint promised works picked for merit and reading fun alike.

Ten beings from beyond space give this brisk tale its hook and title. Paul Fairman, who wrote as Jorgensen, filled it with pulp pace and twists. Strange doubles and hidden foes drive the plot at speed. The book is a neat slice of early 1960s paperback science fiction, built to grip on the first page and not let go.
20936-the-new-society:
Ending the proletarian state can be neared, argues The New Society, by wise laws on property and schooling. Curbs on inheritance rights stand chief among its tools named here. Strict state control, the writer holds, is not required for that end.

Graham Wallas, a Fabian thinker, probes how great societies strain the human mind. Schools, wealth, and modern scale fill his thought on reform without revolt. Wallas wrote for readers who wanted reform. He asks how minds like ours can run states so vast. The book is a work of social thought.
20958-life-in-the-medieval-university:
Logic by Aristotle, sums by Boethius, and Euclid's geometry ruled the medieval schools, Robert S. Rait notes. Ptolemy stands for astronomy, though mixed with kings of his name. Theology crowned the long course that followed the arts degree.

Life in the Medieval University shows how scholars lived, ate, fought, and learned. Paris, Oxford, and Bologna supply tales of gowns, towns, and riots. Rait writes with a scholar's ease on a world half monkish, half rowdy. Students today will know much of it still: debt, lodging hunts, and fierce pride in one's own school and its ways.
21048-just-patty:
Mae Mertelle's financier father takes a hit from Patty Wyatt in Jean Webster's Just Patty, from 1911. Patty's own father, a reform judge, spends his days jailing financiers, she retorts. Her grin turns the proud boast into a shared schoolgirl laugh.

Patty, of Daddy-Long-Legs fame in Webster's wider world, stars in these school tales. Pranks, classes, and chums at St. Ursula's fill the brisk chapters. Webster writes girls with wit, nerve, and warm hearts in equal share. Just Patty shows her at her lightest, a convent school romp by a teller who never talked down to her girls.
21305-a-dash-from-diamond-city:
Two young men are sent from Mafeking with important despatches for the general at Kimberley in George Manville Fenn's Boer War tale. Their road crosses Boer-held country in South Africa, with mishaps at every stage. A side plot follows illicit diamond dealing around the diamond city of the title.

Just before reaching Kimberley the riders are badly wounded and lie unconscious for a fortnight. The despatches, sewn into a filthy, blood-stained jacket, are feared thrown away before they are found safe. Fenn opens in a mud-walled, iron-roofed office with typewriter and pens scratching, then moves out into the veld, where the dash is won or lost.
21772-the-path-of-duty:
An American long settled in London writes out a story for a curious friend in this Henry James tale of 1885. The story concerns Ambrose Tester, and the narrator knew all the parties from the first. He promises a regular development and tells it by a red fire in the December fog. Sixteen years of London life have left him, he says, still sensitive to the city's strangeness.

The title names the tale's pressure: what people owe, and what owing costs them. James builds the story from observation, talk, and small social turns rather than big events. London's bigness and strangeness fill the frame. It is James in his early manner, a moral knot tied slowly in good company.
21839-sense-and-sensibility:
Two sisters stand at the heart of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility, shown here in the 1902 Macmillan edition. One sister is ruled by sense, the other by feeling. Hugh Thomson's drawings, first issued in 1896, fill this printing. The Dashwoods have long been settled at Norland Park in Sussex when the tale begins. A death soon strips the family of home and income, and the sisters must make their way in a narrower world.

Elinor hides her heart while Marianne wears hers openly, and love tests both habits hard. Austen writes courtship as a study in character, with wit in every drawing room. Austin Dobson supplies the introduction. It is Austen's first published novel, and still one of her most loved.
21960-blue-bonnet-s-ranch-party:
A Texas girl takes her friends west in Blue Bonnet's Ranch Party, part of the Blue Bonnet series for girls, issued in 1912. Blue Bonnet's party rides in a private car and still finds the journey to Woodford the longest-seeming ever taken. The frontispiece watches her see the sun rise out of the prairie. Lela Horn Richards and Caroline E. Jacobs created the series, with this sequel written by C. E. Jacobs and Edyth Ellerbeck.

The series ran through Boston, housekeeping, and a debut before and after this ranch visit. Thirteen impressions by 1921 show how girls loved her. John Goss drew the pictures. The book gives its heroine both worlds: Boston polish and a Texas ranch, with the ranch winning the party's heart.
21981-the-essentials-of-spirituality:
What spirituality is, apart from any creed, is Felix Adler's question in The Essentials of Spirituality. Adler, founder of the Ethical Culture movement, begins with hunger: first the felt absence of spirituality, then the search for a higher quality of life. The quality, he argues, may come through belief in a divine father, through Spinoza's pantheism, through Buddhism's Nirvana, or through Ethical Culture itself.

He warns that the word spiritual often serves as a synonym for muddy thought and misty feeling. His remedy is definition joined to portraits of character. The essay is short, calm, and meant for seekers outside the churches. It shows Adler's lifelong project: keeping the moral fire of religion while letting its doctrines go. Few American sermons argue so gently.
22118-official-report-of-the-niger-valle:
Martin R. Delany, a Black abolitionist, doctor, and writer, led an exploring party to West Africa in 1859. His Official Report of the Niger Valley Exploring Party argues the case for emigration. Delany held that Black Americans must win a place of entire equality somewhere. He looked to the Niger valley as a land where a rising generation could rule itself.

The report describes the country, its peoples, its cotton, and its trade. It also answers critics of the emigration plan in strong terms. Delany's mission signed a treaty with Yoruba leaders for settlement land. The document stands as a founding text of Black nationalism, written before the Civil War freed the enslaved.
22239-security:
Security is a science fiction tale of a regimented future and a man saving for escape. Its Lancaster has two assets: his savings and an extra liquor ration. Tonight, coming home through the tube, he decides to make a dent in the whiskey. He ate at the commissary as usual but skipped the talk, thinking of the drink all the way home.

That small rebellion opens a story about control, rationing, and the price of safety. The future here runs on commissary meals, tubes, and allotted pleasures. Pulp writers used such sketches to test how much freedom men trade for security. The tale's chill comes from its quietness: nothing explodes, yet everything is owned.
22585-and-devious-the-line-of-duty:
And Devious the Line of Duty is a science fiction story of war and alliance among future worlds. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its politics turn on Jardeen, a large companion world whose space navy outmatches that of any other single world.

Neutral worlds wait to follow Jardeen's lead, so its choice of allies may decide a war. An alliance between Jardeen and the Verdam People's Worlds would, the narrator warns, quickly end the Terran Republic. The stakes are set out in the clipped style of pulp space opera. Readers who like grand strategy, rival star nations, and old magazine science fiction will find a compact example of the form.
22623-divinity:
Divinity is a science fiction story of a man adrift in space, weighing a desperate escape. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its hero, cut off from his ship and crew, thinks wildly for a moment before the risks of freedom in space come clear to him.

He must reach a civilized port, persuade the authorities he was shipwrecked and parted from his crew, then vanish into the crowd. The dangers are plain, but he takes them: anything beats running out of air and food alone in the dark. The story wrings tension from logistics and loneliness rather than monsters. It is a lean example of the stranded-spaceman tale from the magazine years.
23067-stories-of-animal-sagacity:
Cats and dogs open Stories of Animal Sagacity. The author begins with anecdotes of the sagacity shown by animals all readers know well. Anyone who watches a pet closely, the author says, will recognize the behavior. Readers will think of their own Tabby's tricks, or of a dog at home who once did nearly as clever a thing.

Anecdote follows anecdote, horses, elephants, birds, and more joining the cats and dogs. Each story argues that animals reason, remember, and feel more than people grant. Victorian natural history loved such collections, halfway between science and fireside wonder. The book's charm is its faith in close watching. It invites young readers to test every claim against the pet asleep by their own chair.
23290-the-dogs-dinner-party:
The Dog's Dinner Party is a story told through animals. One guest, a dog charged with watching over and protecting the livestock, fears he must decline his invitation. On second thoughts, he resolves to venture out anyway, since it is not a late dinner.

He can get away early, he reckons. His coat is rather the worse for wear, which troubles him. But he does own one handsome collar, at least. So he accepts. Readers get a genteel animal tale that plays human manners for gentle comedy: duty, dress, and dinner invitations, all weighed by a conscientious dog.
271-black-beauty:
Anna Sewell's Black Beauty tells a horse's life in his own voice, from a meadow colt to a London cab horse. Published in 1877, the novel follows Beauty through kind grooms and cruel masters, fires, accidents, and rest. Ginger, Merrylegs, and John Manly share his chapters.

Sewell, a Quaker invalid, wrote to plead for kinder treatment of horses: better bits, no bearing reins, and rest for tired animals. The book's plain moral force changed stable practice and law. Children still meet it as a first classic. Its plea for mercy outlived its century.
321-moran-of-the-lady-letty:
Frank Norris promises a story of a battle, at least one murder, and several sudden deaths. Moran of the Lady Letty opens, oddly, at a pink tea for debutante Josie Herrick in San Francisco. Ross Wilbur arrives too early and faces a terrifying array of millinery.

Wilbur is soon shanghaied aboard the Lady Letty, where Captain Moran rules a brutal crew. The pink-tea world gives way to forecastles, storms, and murder. Norris dedicated the book to a life-saving captain. The novel mixes society comedy with sea adventure. Norris's sea tale followed his California novels of greed and fate.
356-beyond-the-city:
Arthur Conan Doyle sets this gentle novel in a row of new villas on the edge of London. Two elderly sisters watch their neighbors with keen, kind curiosity, and the arrival of new folk at number three stirs talk. Soon a retired admiral, a doctor, and a young couple fill the street with fresh life.

Gossip, courtship, and small town manners drive the plot, with a darker note when past deeds catch up with one resident. Doyle writes with warmth and humor, far from his detective tales. The book charms as a portrait of late Victorian suburb life, where news travels fast over garden fences.
783-the-lost-city:
Joseph E. Badger Jr. wrote this adventure of Professor Featherwit, a man of science whose notes and experiments lead him to an unknown land. A tornado lifts his party into strange country, where a duel, a queer fish, and unwelcome visitors test their wits. The lost city of the title waits beyond the wilds.

Badger writes in the dime-novel style, with brisk chapters, bold perils, and a hero who thinks his way out of trouble. The tale mixes science fancy with frontier adventure, in the spirit of Verne. It charms readers who enjoy old-fashioned lost-world yarns, where each chapter ends with a fresh wonder or danger.
862-philosophy-4-a-story-of-harvard-univ:
Owen Wister wrote this story of Harvard, centred on the course called Philosophy 4 and the young men who take it. Two frowning boys in tennis flannels sit beneath lamp and gas, listening with gloomy hunger to a third who tutors them. The scene sets a tale of college work, friendship, and honour.

Wister, himself a Harvard man, writes with humour and affection for undergraduate life, its clubs, its codes, and its trials. The story turns on what young men owe each other and their college, when study and sport collide. It offers a vivid, old-fashioned portrait of Harvard at the turn of the century.
889-two-years-in-the-forbidden-city:
Princess Der Ling, first lady in waiting to the Empress Dowager of China, wrote this memoir of two years inside the Forbidden City. Daughter of Lord Yu Keng of the Manchu White Banner, she entered court life with a rare insider's view, and she dedicates the book to her beloved father.

Der Ling describes the Empress Dowager, court rites, dress, food, and daily routine, with anecdotes that humanise a secluded world. Her account, written for Western readers, blends admiration with candour. The book remains a vivid, first-hand portrait of late Qing court life, just before its fall.
917-barnaby-rudge-a-tale-of-the-riots-of:
Charles Dickens wrote this historical novel about the Gordon Riots of 1780, when London mobs rose against Catholic relief and burned the city for days. Barnaby Rudge, a simple young man with a pet raven named Grip, is drawn into the riots, while his father hides a darker past.

Dickens mixes a murder mystery with the history of the mob, showing how fear and rumour turn crowds to fire. The novel's London, from quiet homes to burning prisons, is vividly drawn. Barnaby Rudge stands as Dickens's first historical novel, and a powerful study of riot, madness, and loyalty.
a-beleaguered-city:
Margaret Oliphant, a Scots writer of great range, wrote this strange tale of a French town in 1880. The town is Semur, a quiet place of old homes and slow days. Oliphant was famed for sober tales of real life, which makes this book stand out.

The dead of the town rise and come back, in a calm and grave host. They drive the living from their homes, yet do no harm and speak no word that men can grasp. The tale's power lies in its hush: a siege by ghosts, told with rare weight and calm.
a-district-messenger-boy-and-a-necktie-p:
A District Messenger Boy and A Necktie Party, by James Otis, collects short tales for boys from the author of Toby Tyler. The first opens in a messenger office, where Joe Curtis, number two hundred ninety seven, receives exact orders from a traveler. He must take tickets to the Sound steamer, claim the key of a paid stateroom, and stow two satchels before the boat sails for Providence within the hour.

From that errand grows the tale of the unwilling passengers, and a second story, Dan Hardy's Crippy, fills out the first half. A Necktie Party then runs three chapters of rival schemes by Si, Aggie, and Tom, each plotting around the same social prize. Otis, who wrote working boys' lives by the shelf, keeps the machinery light: errands, steamers, and party tricks, with every boy's competence quietly on trial.
a-woman-of-thirty:
Honoré de Balzac begins on a bright Sunday morning in April 1813, in Ellen Marriage's translation, as a worried father hands his beautiful young daughter down from a carriage in Paris. The first part, called Early Mistakes, follows her into a marriage chosen for rank rather than love. Her life becomes the book's long study.

In linked episodes Balzac follows the woman through young love, boredom, a lover, children, loss, and age, watching how each stage changes her heart. Few novels of the period treat a woman's inner life so fully or so unsparingly. The title fixed a phrase in French culture: the woman of thirty, at the height of her powers and sorrows.
an-exhortation-to-peace-and-unity:
John Bunyan's treatise takes its text from Ephesians: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. An editorial note in this 1845 printing admits the work's genuineness has been questioned, yet prints it with the collected works, as most editions do. The voice that speaks is Bunyan's in manner, plain and urgent.

Religion, the treatise argues, is the great bond of human society, and it shames Christians when religion itself is split by strife. The writer pleads with believers who hold one Lord, one faith, and one baptism to stop wounding each other over lesser things. The tract is short, warm, and practical, aimed at church quarrels of Bunyan's own hard century.
australian-search-party:
Charles H. Eden's Australian Search Party, reprinted from H. W. Bates's Illustrated Travels, begins with a cyclone. In the autumn of 1866 a storm nearly destroyed Cardwell and Townsville on Queensland's north-east coast. Among its losses was the schooner Eva, bound for Rockingham Bay with passengers and cargo. Then came a report of white men seen among the tribes near the Herbert River. Only those who have visited Australia, Eden writes, can picture such captivity's horror. A search party went out to learn the truth.

Eden narrates the expedition into the ranges and scrubs. His pages mix geography, danger, and the period's hard assumptions about the frontier. Readers get a primary document of Australian exploration literature: a rescue that became a survey of unknown country, written by a participant for Bates's great popular record of discovery and adventure.
b09-luther-address-nobility:
Martin Luther aimed his 1520 address, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, straight at the princes of Germany. He argued that Rome had built three walls to guard its power from reform. Behind them, Rome claimed that church rule outranks earthly rule. It claimed that only Rome can read Scripture, and only the pope can call a council.

Luther knocks down each wall in turn and calls on the nobility to act. The address gave the Reformation a clear public program, in German, for lay rulers to carry out. It also stands as a founding text of German national feeling. Few pamphlets of the age reached so far.
b09-luther-babylonian-captivity:
On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, published by Martin Luther in 1520, takes its title from the exile of Israel in Babylon. Luther casts the church of Rome as the captor and the sacraments as the captives. The Latin treatise was the boldest of the three great tracts he issued that year.

Luther cuts the seven sacraments of the old church down to two that he finds clearly set by Christ, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Penance holds a partial place in his scheme. The attack struck at the core of priestly power over daily life. It forms the doctrinal heart of the break with Rome.
barnaby-rudge-a-tale-of-the-riots-of-eig:
Charles Dickens wrote Barnaby Rudge as a tale of the riots of eighty, the Gordon Riots of 1780, and prefaced it with an essay on ravens drawn from two birds he owned. The simple-minded Barnaby, his mother, and his talking raven Grip stand near a fifteen-year-old murder mystery at the Warren. Locksmith Gabriel Varden and his apprentice Joe carry the respectable side of the story.

Secret marriages, a runaway son defended against his mother's scorn, and Protestant mobs marching on London build toward the riots' fire and slaughter. Dickens, writing early in his career, made this his first historical novel. Its crowd scenes and study of fanaticism still impress, and Grip later echoed into Poe's famous raven.
beasley-s-christmas-party:
Beasley's Christmas Party, by Booth Tarkington, follows a young newspaperman through his first days in a state capital. Tarkington dates the tale October 1909 and dedicates it to the poet James Whitcomb Riley. The narrator returns at four in the morning from his first night's work on the Wainwright Morning Despatch. Moonlit streets lie still as a country Sunday. He passes the house he most admires in the city.

He has just taken a room next door at Mrs Apperthwaite's, and counts the fine house almost a citizen's possession. From that doorstep he is drawn into the world of Beasley, a local magnate. Beasley's Christmas party mixes politics, money, and a household secret. The secret involves an imaginary companion. Tarkington tells it as comedy with a sting: a small capital's great man, a reporter's education, and the season when every performance of generosity is also a move in the game.
beyond-the-city:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote Beyond the City in 1892, a short novel of the new suburbs south of London, written between his Sherlock Holmes tales. It opens with two elderly sisters, Monica and Bertha, watching from behind their curtain as new neighbors move into the villa across the road. The newcomers, a widow's household lately rich from India, stir the quiet street of three neat houses.

Courtships form among the young people, money worries surface, and a secret from the Indian past works its way into the present. Doyle, who lived in such a suburb himself at Norwood, draws the tea tables, lawns, and gossip with affection and a light sting. The tale shows his gift working without a detective to lead it.
black-beauty:
Anna Sewell wrote Black Beauty, published in 1877, her only book, written in ill health during the last years of her life. The story is told by the horse himself. Beauty begins as a glossy black colt on a kind farm. He learns his lessons from his mother. Then he is sold from home to home. Some owners are kind, and some are careless. He works as a carriage horse, a cab horse in London, and a cart horse worn nearly to death.

His stable mates, merry Merrylegs and high-spirited Ginger, meet fates of their own. Sewell wrote the book to protest cruelty to horses. She hated the tight bearing rein then in fashion. The book changed how a nation treated its animals, and it still speaks for them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-administrator:
An administrator of church property is one charged with the care of church goods. Supreme administrative authority over all church temporalities rests with the Sovereign Pontiff, by his primacy of jurisdiction. The pope's power here is solely administrative, since he cannot properly be called owner of goods belonging to the universal church or particular churches.

Pontifical authority works chiefly via the Propaganda, St. Peter's Fabrica, the Camera Apostolica, and the Cardinal Camerlengo, and appears in decrees of councils worldwide. In each diocese, administration rests primarily with the bishop, subject to the Holy See, and all inferior administrators depend on him unless exempted by law, as with religious orders. Parish priests bear an important share of this duty, and councils urge administrators to secure titles under secular law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cavity:
The altar cavity is a small chamber, square or oblong, in the altar's body holding relics of two canonized martyrs. One martyr's relic alone still makes the consecration valid, and other saints' relics may be added, especially the saint honoured by the church. The relics must be real portions of the saints' bodies, not merely of their garments.

The chamber may sit at the altar's front or back, midway between table and foot, or in the table's centre near the front edge. A bevelled stone slab fits exactly over the opening when the first or second place is chosen. Sealed within, the relics belong to the altar's consecration rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amovibility:
Canon law gives the name amovibility to the state of church officers who can be removed from their posts at a bishop's will. Most rectors in the United States and England fall in this class. Parish assistants, vicars-general, archdeacons, and rural deans belong there too, while holders of perpetual dignities can lose office only in set cases.

Canonists long argued over whether a bishop could remove such a man without cause. Exceptions arose where hatred, damage to a good name, or harm to a parish was involved. The article sets out the limits on that power and the right of recourse to a higher authority. It also gives the procedure laid down for the United States by the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore and later Roman instructions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-maj:
Apostolic Majesty is a title borne by the kings of Hungary. It has been used since Maria Theresa's time by the king himself and in letters addressed to him by officials and private persons. Its supposed origin lies with St. Stephen, said to have gained it from Pope Sylvester II for spreading Christianity in Hungary. Hartvik, Stephen's biographer, reports the pope hailing him as a veritable apostle of Christ for his holy labours in the faith.

Yet Sylvester's bull of 27 March 1000 granted Stephen crown and royal title. It also returned the kingdom he had offered to Rome and gave him the right to have the cross borne before him with authority over bishoprics. Even so, it gives no basis for this particular title. Moreover, that bull is proved a forgery later than 1574. The entry thus separates a proud royal style from the shaky document once used to support it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolicity:
Apostolicity is the mark by which today's church is recognized as identical with the church Jesus founded upon the apostles. It matters most, the article argues, because it is the surest sign of the true church, the easiest to examine, and it virtually contains unity, sanctity, and catholicity. Apostolic is preferred to Christian because it links church to Christ its founder and to the apostles.

An apostle is one sent by Christ's authority to continue his mission, above all a member of the Twelve. Apostolicity of doctrine and of mission are both required. Doctrine demands that the deposit of faith entrusted to the apostles be kept whole, and mission demands a line of envoys from them. The entry gives the Catholic logic of a church that claims to be not merely old, but apostolic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
An archconfraternity is a group empowered to affiliate other groups of the same kind and to share with them its indulgences and privileges. The article sets out what a reader needs to grasp the general subject. It covers what must come first, the rules for joining, the usual method of the process, and a list of the main groups.

To gain indulgences, the group to be joined must first be approved and given legal existence by proper church authority. Archconfraternities do not set groups up; they merely join them. That approval normally belongs to the local bishop, though heads of certain religious orders hold the power for many groups, above all in mission lands or abnormal conditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aseity:
Aseity, from Latin a, from, and se, itself, meaning being from itself, is the property by which a being subsists of and from itself. It belongs, and can belong only, to God, the article argues. Seeking the efficient, exemplary, and final cause of every thing, of their existence, nature, and organization, we reach at last a Being. He depends for existence, realization, or end on no cause but himself. He holds within himself his own reason for being.

That property of absolute independence, or self-existence in nature, is what we call aseity. The notion holds a negative and a positive side, absolute independence and self-existence, which together form one single objective property. The Catholic concept presents God as independent and self-existent by nature, not merely uncaused by accident, and the entry unpacks a short Latin term into a whole doctrine of God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-bonn:
Augustin Bonnetty was a French writer born at Entrevaux in 1798 who died at Paris in 1879. He entered the Digne seminary in 1815, but, too young for ordination, he tutored a family at Marseilles. He soon felt his mission was to defend the Church with science and philosophy while remaining a layman. In Paris in 1830 he founded the Annales de Philosophie Chretienne, which he edited until his death. Its aim was to show the agreement of science and religion.

A chief theme was a primitive revelation, said to be visible even in the myths of all nations. Bonnetty pressed this idea too far, stressing revelation and slighting reason, a drift toward traditionalism that drew Rome's notice. In 1855 he was asked to sign four propositions guarding reason's role in reaching truth. His books included Beauties of Church History, Christianity and Philosophy, and a translation of Premare's traces of Christian dogma in Chinese books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baker-city:
Baker City is a diocese covering fifteen Oregon counties, an area of 65,683 square miles. It was established in 1903, and Charles J. O'Reilly became its first bishop that year. O'Reilly, rector of Portland's Immaculate Heart of Mary and editor of the Catholic Sentinel, was consecrated on 25 August. The diocese counted about 4,000 Catholics, served by ten diocesan and seven Franciscan and Jesuit priests.

Sisters of St Francis, St Dominic, and the Holy Name ran five schools and academies. At the Umatilla reservation, over 500 Catholic Indians were served by Jesuits, two teaching brothers, and eight Franciscan sisters. The diocese held thirteen churches and thirty-six mission stations. O'Reilly was born at St John, New Brunswick, in 1862, studied at Montreal's Grand Seminary, and was ordained at Portland in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capital-punis:
Capital punishment is death inflicted by lawful process as a penalty for crime. The entry traces the practice from the earliest human history through ancient Israel and Rome to modern states. The Latin word capitalis, tied to caput or head, covered whatever touched life itself. The entry opens with Cain's fratricide and the decree of Genesis 9:6. It follows with the many capital offenses in the law given to Israel.

Later sections follow Roman statutes on poisoning and conspiracy and English witchcraft laws that claimed thousands of victims. They note canon law's bar on clerics shedding blood. They weigh reformers such as Beccaria and Voltaire against the penalty. The entry closes with methods around the world, from beheading in Switzerland and Prussia to shooting in Ecuador and Oldenburg. Spain used the garrotte, and China strangled offenders in public.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chastity:
An entry on chastity as a virtue, the control of sexual appetite by reason, treated here apart from celibacy and virginity, which have their own articles. Chastity belongs to temperance, the virtue that governs pleasures, and stands beside abstinence and sobriety, which govern food and drink. It is often confused with modesty, but modesty is properly its outpost and safeguard, a reserve about acts that cause shame.

Aristotle marked a line between chastity and continence. The entry traces the virtue from nature, where reason alone checks appetite, to faith, where the body is honoured as the temple of the Holy Spirit. It surveys Greek and Roman practice, where sexual licence was open and marriage lightly broken. Christian practice then made chastity stern and austere, through the example of Christ and the image of marriage as the union of Christ and the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christianity:
A vast entry on Christianity as a religion, setting out its origin, its relation to other faiths, and its essential nature. It leaves doctrines in detail and the Church as a visible organisation to separate articles. It speaks of the Christianity realised in the Catholic Church alone, not of non-Catholic sects.

Its sources are chiefly the New Testament and writings just after the apostles, whose authenticity the entry takes as largely granted, as historians grant Caesar on Gaul or Tacitus on Rome. It notes that mature non-Catholic critics now place the Gospels, Acts, and most Epistles in the apostolic age. Harnack is quoted on the fullness of tradition already present under Trajan, between 98 and 117.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-proper:
An entry on church property, defending the Church's right to acquire and hold temporal goods. Though acted on everywhere, that right met contradictors: Arnold of Brescia, the Waldenses, Marsilius of Padua, and the Wycliffites held that Gospel ministers should own nothing. John the Twenty-second answered Marsilius in 1323, affirming that Christ and the apostles truly owned what they held and that church goods were not at the emperor's disposal.

Constance condemned Wyclif and Hus, defining that churchmen may hold possessions without sin and that civil seizure counts as sacrilege. Pius the Ninth reaffirmed the point in Quanta Cura of 1864, rejecting any claim that state ownership of all church property squares with theology or canon law. Beyond decrees, the entry grounds the right in reason and tradition: a visible society with public duties needs temporal means, and gifts bestowed on the Church remain under her control.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-authori:
Civil authority, the moral power of command, is backed when needed by physical coercion over its members, exercised by the State. The article treats its nature, sources, limits, divisions, and origin, with true and false theories. Authority is natural to man because man naturally lives in society, and society holds together only under authority. Even professed anarchists, it argues, treat anarchy as a temporary step toward their own rule.

Forms of government vary endlessly: monarchies, aristocracies, and democracies, direct like ancient Athens or representative like the United States. The fixed point is that the authority actually existing must be obeyed, since refusing it means refusing authority itself. The article then weighs contract theories, including Hobbes and his Leviathan and Rousseau and his General Will, against the older teaching on authority's origin and bounds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-incorpo:
Christianity found the corporation already developed under Roman law and adapted it early to hold and transmit church property. Second- and third-century burial societies served this end, and great medieval monasteries were organised as corporations. Mortmain law shows how secure this tenure proved amid feudal warfare. Canon lawyers refined the idea into the corporation sole: a bishop, vicar, or pastor who succeeds to an office and its temporal goods alone.

In England corporations arise by prescription, charter, or parliamentary Act; in the United States a state legislature creates them. American law treats church and incorporated religious society as different things, the society handling temporal goods. Title often stays with the bishop in fee simple, but states trend toward incorporation, as in New York in 1863 and Michigan in 1897. English Catholics before the Charity Act of 1832 could only trust private holders, with no legal remedy if they misused a bequest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clandestinity:
Clandestinity is the matrimonial impediment Trent introduced by the decree Tametsi. Anyone attempting marriage otherwise than before the parish priest, or another priest with his or the ordinary's leave, and before two or three witnesses, is rendered incapable of the contract. Such a contract is null and void. The council upheld earlier clandestine marriages until annulled, yet declared the Church always abhorred and prohibited them.

That antipathy runs back to Ignatius of Antioch, who urged marriage with the bishop's consent, and to Tertullian, who judged unions without church authority near fornication. A Fourth Council of Carthage canon, so called, required presentation to a priest for blessing. The decree's reach varied with promulgation. It was never published in England, Scotland, or Scandinavia, and Benedict the Fourteenth settled its application to Dutch heretics. Delegation of the priest's faculty, special or general, raised further questions of validity and liceity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-columbia-univ:
John McGinn's entry describes Columbia University at Portland, Oregon, not the New York school of the same name. It stands on the east bank of the Willamette in northern Portland. The Congregation of Holy Cross runs it, from its mother-house at Notre Dame, Indiana. In 1898 Portland University, run by a local Methodist group, failed and closed. Its buildings stood empty for three years. In 1901 Archbishop Alexander Christie bought the property for the diocese.

For one year diocesan clergy ran the school, now called Columbia University. In 1902 Christie asked the Holy Cross provincial, Rev. J. A. Zahm, for teachers, and religious soon took charge. The university gained incorporation under Oregon law in 1909, with power to grant degrees in arts, sciences, and letters. By 1912 about two hundred students studied there under twenty professors. New Christie Hall added room for one hundred and fifty more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraternity:
William Fanning's entry defines a confraternity or sodality, from Latin confraternitas, as a voluntary association of the faithful. Competent church authority erects and guides it for special works of Christian charity or piety. Pious unions resemble confraternities, but differ in two ways. They need not be canonically erected. They also seek the neighbor's good rather than members' personal sanctification. Confraternities split into those properly so called and those bearing the name by extension.

Both kinds rise by canonical authority. Proper confraternities hold a more precise organization, with rights and duties set by church law. Members often wear a peculiar costume and recite the Office together. When a confraternity gains power to aggregate other sodalities, its reach widens further. Lay associations of this sort stood at Constantinople and Alexandria in very ancient times. Clement VIII's constitution of 7 December 1604, later modified, still frames much of their law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Brother Philemon's entry follows the Brothers of Charity, founded in Belgium early in the present century. Leo XIII approved and confirmed rule and constitutions on 4 July 1899. Founder Pierre J. Triest, titular canon of Saint Bavon of Ghent, earned the name Vincent de Paul of his country for charity's service, winning three royal decorations with the land's highest civic orders. After his death countrymen raised a superb Brussels mausoleum in his honor.

The congregation aims first at members' sanctification in religious life through charity embracing every phase of moral and physical suffering and want. Works center on tending the sick, sheltering poor workmen, and caring for the aged and the insane. Government rests with a superior general at Ghent, cradle of the congregation, aided by a four-member central council, assistant visitors, a general secretary, and a general procurator.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consanguinity:
Richard Burtsell's entry defines consanguinity as a marriage impediment reaching the fourth degree inclusive. The term means blood-relationship, the bond between persons descended from the same stock, within limits set by nature, God, or State or Church. Since all men descend from one stock, limitation points to the nearest root.

Descent of one from another forms the direct line; shared blood from a common ancestor, the collateral. History traces groups marrying within themselves, early Rome forbidding cousin marriage, though frequent after the Second Punic War, with discipline continuing to the eighth century. A Germanic computation, like Germanic inheritance reckoning, shaped later counting. Gregory I, if the letter is truly his, let Anglo-Saxons rest at the fourth degree. Motives joined recognition of Roman prohibitions with extension beyond them. Calculation weighs line, degree, and stock: direct line counts generations, while Uniat Churches forbid collateral marriage to the seventh degree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creighton-uni:
An institutional entry describes Creighton University at Omaha, Nebraska, conducted by the Jesuit Fathers. It comprised high school and college classes, a free classical day college, and schools covering medicine, dentistry, pharmacy, and law. In 1907-08 its faculty numbered 104, and attendance ran near 800.

Creighton ranked as the first free Catholic college in the country. Edward Creighton had planned a free school for higher education but died intestate before providing for it. His widow Mary Lucretia carried out his intention by a bequest near 200,000 dollars. The university's free dispensary and dental infirmary served thousands yearly, and its hospital treated about 2,400 patients a year, over half of them non-Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-moriart:
A biographical entry follows David Moriarty, Bishop of Kerry and pulpit orator, born at Ardfert in 1812 and dead in 1877. Schooled in his native diocese and at Boulogne, he passed to Maynooth, spent two years in the Dunboyne establishment, and served four years as vice-president of the Irish College in Paris. His success there won him the presidency of All Hallows missionary college in Dublin.

There his noble oratory, chaste, elevated, varied, and convincing, became famous. Made coadjutor of Kerry in 1854, he succeeded in 1856, building churches, schools, a diocesan college, and convents. His Allocutions to the Clergy show profound thought in oratorical style. A patriot in O'Connell's mould, he nonetheless denounced Fenianism strongly, running counter to popular feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-de-paul-unive:
An institutional entry traces De Paul University in Chicago from Saint Vincent's College, opened in September 1898. Archbishop Feehan wanted a Catholic college for young men on Chicago's North Side, and Vincentian priests incorporated Saint Vincent's in June 1898. Engineering courses began in 1906, and the university itself was incorporated on Christmas Day 1907 by ten Vincentian priests and five Catholic laymen.

Besides collegiate studies, De Paul offered mechanical, civil, and electrical engineering and special science work, with thirteen priests and six laymen on faculty. Under Rector McCabe from July 1910, it opened degrees to women through its 1911 summer school, attended by one hundred sisters and lay teachers. In spring 1912 the Illinois College of Law joined as its law department, adding 150 students to a total of 550.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deity:
A comparative religion entry treats the non-Christian notion of deity, reserving the Christian idea for the article on God. It opens with the word's roots: Sanskrit dyaus, bright sky, yielding deva, bright beings, and kin words from Zeus to Jupiter, Diana, and Juno. History's earliest documents already show religion long established, with deities adored and sacrifices offered beyond memory.

Sections trace several paths to many gods. Nature powers were made human in form. Heroes rose to godhead by apotheosis. Augustine saw Rome's many gods melt into one Jupiter. Politics added gods as tribes joined or conquerors displaced old gods. Language itself shaped divine names. The entry closes with early monotheistic traces in the Rig-Veda and modern anthropological theories of Tylor and Spencer, judging them against the facts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duty:
Duty, as lexicographers define it, is something due, a service one is bound to perform or to shun. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds a second sense, the unique stir of conscience voiced in the words ought, bound, and moral obligation. When a person judges I ought to do it, the judgment is felt not as mere statement nor as mere preference. It presses as imperative and magisterial, with a feeling that drives toward action.

The entry analyzes this datum of conscience at length, moving from personal duty to duties toward God, neighbor, and civil society. Since God wills civil society for the growth of human nature, he wills the authority without which it cannot stand. Since lower animals cannot hold rights, no duties are owed to them, though duties to God touch them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ellen-whitty:
Ellen Whitty, in religion Mary Vincent, was a Sister of Mercy who planted the order in Queensland, born near Wexford in 1819 and dead at Brisbane in 1892. She was a chief helper of Mother Catherine McAuley in founding the Institute of the Sisters of Mercy. In 1839 she joined the young community in Baggot Street, Dublin, was trained by the foundress, became mistress of novices in 1844, and superior-general in 1849.

During the Crimean War she offered her nuns to nurse sick and wounded soldiers, and her sister Mary Agnes went to the front. In 1861 Bishop James Quinn of Brisbane, whose vast new diocese held only two priests and four churches, appealed for help. Mother Whitty led her sisters to Queensland, landing on 10 May 1861, and laboured there for the rest of her life, founding more than twenty convents before her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eternity:
Boetius defines eternity as the complete, succession-free possession of endless life. The definition, adopted by the Schoolmen for God's eternity, implies four things: a life without beginning, end, or succession, and of the most perfect kind. God not only is or exists, but lives. Applied to God, the notion of life, like every abstract notion, remains only analogous.

He does not live or exist precisely as anything else we know. Our notions of life and existence come from creatures, where life implies change and existence is added to essence. In God there can be no composition or change or imperfection, but all is pure act or being. The agnostic is not thereby justified in saying we can know nothing of God. Yet the agnostic, arguing this way, still thinks and speaks of Him as really as we do.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-falsity:
Falsity means a wilful perversion of truth, in words or in deeds. Its forms include counterfeiting, false weights, false measures, bribery, and forgery. Tampering with a will counts among its graver and more harmful instances. The article treats falsity as a sin against truth, justice, and neighbourly trust.

Canon law punished forgery of papal letters with excommunication. Pius IX renewed that penalty in his constitution Apostolicae Sedis. A person who profits by falsity must make full restitution in conscience. The article weighs excuses, ignorance, good faith, and the duty to repair harm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fordham-unive:
Fordham University in New York grew out of St. John's College, opened on Rose Hill Farm at Fordham on 24 June 1841 by Bishop Hughes. Its theological seminary had moved there the same year from Lafargeville, and the New York legislature gave it degree-granting powers in April 1846. Two months later the Jesuits bought the property from the diocese, and Augustus Thebaud became its first Jesuit president.

Early enrolment rose and fell with the times, dipping during the Civil War and reaching about 500 students early in the new century. A law school and a medical school opened in 1904 under President John Collins. By 1912 the university counted 548 students under 124 professors, spread across law, medicine, and the academic department, with its own press publishing historical work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaston-jean-b:
Gaston de Renty, a French layman born in Normandy in 1611, gave up court, army, and politics for the poor. Only son of Baron de Renty, he studied at the Collège de Navarre and the Jesuits at Caen, finishing at seventeen at the College of Nobles. He wrote treatises on mathematics, in which he excelled, before the Imitation of Christ turned his mind toward holiness.

Though he wished to become a Carthusian, he married at his parents' wish. In 1638 he left public life for works of mercy, teaching catechism to travelers sheltering at Saint Gervaise Hospital in Paris. With Henry Michael Buch he founded the Brother Shoemakers, honest workmen who shared earnings with the poor. Nine years after his death in 1649, his body was found intact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georgetown-un:
Georgetown University, in Washington, is the United States' oldest Catholic school of higher learning. Founded just after the Revolutionary War by Maryland's incorporated Catholic clergy, it chose trustees empowered to name a president and professors. It has stood under the Society of Jesus since 1805. Its chronicles reach back to earlier Maryland Jesuit schools, conducted by stealth under laws against Catholic education.

John Carroll, who had schooled at Bohemia in Cecil County, forms the moral and personal link to those schools and to Georgetown itself. He drew the plan, issued a prospectus seeking English aid, and chose the site at Georgetown, then chief borough of Montgomery County, Maryland. The college marked its hundredth anniversary with pomp in 1889 and keeps Founder's Day each January in Carroll's honor, with his portrait, missal, and letters among its treasures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hair-in-chris:
Hair and head-dress in Christian antiquity are surveyed here from catacomb paintings to the age of wigs, with texts and monuments as the only safe guide. Early Christians simply followed their times: short hair for men, waved tresses for women, curled and tiered by the late second century. Images of Christ kept long hair parted in the middle and the Virgin kept her veil.

Byzantine mosaics show medium hair cut square across the brow, with jewelled crowns for emperors and closed crowns for bishops. Barbarians let their hair fall free until councils from Patrick's synod of 456 to Rome in 743 forced clerics to cut theirs short. Later fashions run from shaven crowns and long curls to the cautious clerical wig, baring only the tonsure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heredity:
Heredity, the drift of offspring to resemble parents, is paired with change, the common variety that accompanies likeness. Two methods study them: the counting method, working in numbers. The method of Abbot Mendel of Brünn, whose lost notes promise most toward an answer, above all on return. In a splitting one-celled organism heredity is simple, since both daughter cells are parts of the parent cell; sexual breeding tangles it.

Weismann's germ-plasm theory holds that each one combines body plasm with germ plasm, set aside early, stored in the sex gland, undying. The article weighs this against regrowth, where a cut hydra or begonia cutting makes new ones, and finds the theory weakened. Darwin's pangenesis, saying bodily fragments gather in sex cells, rests on no evidence and demands vast works. Hering's hidden memory and legacy of acquired traits remain contested, wounds proving marks are not passed on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heroic-act-of:
The Heroic Act of Charity is a devout offering for the souls in purgatory. A Christian gives God all the good works of his lifetime and all the suffrages that may come to him after death. The act stands defined by a decree dated 18 December 1885 from the Sacred Congregation of Indulgences, confirmed by Leo XIII the next day. One may make it using a set formula or simply through an act of will.

Many who practise it place their merits in the hands of the Blessed Virgin, following the advice of the Theatine Father Gaspar Olider. She may then distribute them as she pleases. Though often called a vow, the act is really an offering and, unlike a vow, it can be revoked at will. A separate vow never to revoke it would probably bind, the entry explains, because a person can dispose of his own will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospitality:
Hospitality, as the church teaches it, means welcoming guests with alacrity and kindness, since those who cherish guests receive Christ in their persons. The Council of Trent enjoined all holders of church benefices, secular or regular, to practise it as far as revenues allowed, following a duty frequently commended by the holy Fathers.

The burden falls chiefly on two classes. Bishops bear it as pastors of the people and as ancient administrators of the faithful's offerings: Gregory's fourfold division gave the bishop's household a portion expressly for hospitality. Religious, above all monks who renounced worldly goods to serve others, bear it as a work of mercy. The entry traces episcopal and monastic hospitality through canon law and custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humility:
Humility means lowliness or submissiveness, from the Latin humilitas, or as Thomas says, from humus, the earth beneath us. Applied to persons and things it can mean what is abject, ignoble, or poor, as in humble birth or a humble dwelling. It can also mean afflictions inflicted by others, when one person humiliates another by pain or suffering.

In its higher ethical sense, the virtue treated here, humility is a modest estimate of one's own worth joined with submission to others. Bernard defines it as a virtue by which a person knowing himself as he truly is holds a lowly view of himself. He willingly submits to God and to others for God's sake. No one else can humiliate a person in this sense; only the person himself can, and properly only with divine grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-immortality:
By immortality people usually mean this doctrine: after death, the human soul lives on in endless conscious existence. Alongside the question of God's existence, it forms the greatest issue philosophy has to deal with. Rational psychology and the philosophy of religion claim it first, though it also brushes against other philosophical fields and a few natural sciences.

Some sort of future life has been believed in, it seems, nearly everywhere and always. Here and there individuals have rejected it, and some religions and philosophical systems clash with it logically yet still have followers. Still, views among different peoples as to the life beyond the grave may have been vague and inconsistent. Yet belief in a future existence seems so far hard to root out from the human race as a whole.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-immunity:
Immunity, from Latin immunitas, means freedom from a legal duty imposed on a person or property by law, custom, or a superior's order. Such freedom counts as a privilege, then, and obeys the same rules. Church usage gives the name to legal freedoms favouring holy places and holy things, Church property, and Church persons.

Look past the changing cases across times and countries to the principle itself: immunity is Church persons' and property's freedom from secular courts. This principle varies necessarily in application according to circumstances. In societies with strong ranks, for instance feudal society, immunities play an important part. In modern society, where men stand much more on a basis of equality, they are less useful. The strong central state power looks on them with disfavour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-individual-in:
Thomas Aquinas supplies the starting point for this philosophy entry: an individual is a being undivided in itself yet set apart from other beings. Individuality is then the set of traits by which a thing holds that unity and keeps its separateness. The entry asks what actually makes a thing an individual, a problem that has taxed the great schools of thought.

Metaphysics comes first, with the world seen as a crowd of distinct things, from stones and animals to men, each recognized as its own. Psychology follows, since mind and self raise the same question from within. The entry closes by noting what individuality means for ethics and for teaching. It is a compact guide to a wide question, not a verdict on it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infallibility:
Freedom from error in final teaching on faith and morals is the claim this long theology entry defends for the Church. Infallibility here means a gift of divine help that guards the Church's definitive dogmatic teaching, not a promise that every churchman is always right. The entry lays out its case under five heads: what the claim means, its proofs, its organs, its scope, and which teachings it covers.

Its organs are ecumenical councils and the pope. Much of the entry weighs how the two relate. It tests hard cases from history such as Liberius, Honorius, Vigilius, and Galileo. Only strictly definitive sentences carry the guarantee, the entry stresses, while supporting argument in a judgment does not. Readers get the full Catholic case, with its limits stated as carefully as its claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infinity:
That which has no end, limit, or boundary is the idea this philosophy and theology entry explores. No finite measure, however often applied, can take in the infinite. No piling up of finite amounts can reach it. Taking finite amounts away cannot exhaust it. Though the word sounds negative, the entry argues it affirms the highest reality, since denying bounds, which are themselves negations, leaves a double negation.

Space and time give the term its first use, but it also applies to perfections such as wisdom, beauty, power, and fullness of being. The entry warns against mixing up infinity with “all-being,” since an infinite being lacks nothing that belongs to its perfection. Readers get a careful definition first, then the theological weight the idea carries in Christian thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-insanity:
No strict, fully satisfying definition of insanity exists, this entry admits at the start, since sanity shades into madness through a borderland that resists sharp lines. A definition that tries to be complete risks sweeping in states that are not madness at all, such as hysteria, fever delirium, or twisted passions. The Century Dictionary's wording is offered as about the best available.

That definition calls insanity a grave harm to the mind's powers. Those powers are intellect, feeling, and will, or one or more of them. Short-lived states caused by drink or acute fever fall outside it. Sorting kinds of insanity proves just as hard, since no single principle of sorting works cleanly. The entry weighs those problems for readers interested in law, morals, and medicine alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-inventory-of-:
A systematic list, item by item, of a person's or institution's goods, rights, titles, and papers is what an inventory means here, from the Latin inventarium. Law requires such lists to keep trustees honest: an inventory is drawn up when management begins. When it ends the outgoing official must produce everything listed or added since, except what was used up or worn out. An authorized official, a notary, or witnesses then check it.

Church property could hardly escape so useful a safeguard. The entry sets out how church rules adapted the civil practice to parishes, dioceses, and religious houses. Readers learn why a dull list matters: it fixes what a steward received, what he must hand back, and where gaps in the record point to fault.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irregularity:
A bar to taking holy orders, or to using orders already received, is what canon law calls irregularity, from a Latin root meaning not according to rule. Canons set the marks for lawful ordination. Those marks are moral probity, proper age, legitimate birth, and knowledge fitted to each order. They also include soundness of body, mind, will, and faith. A defect in any prescribed mark counts as an irregularity. Its direct effect is twofold.

First it forbids receiving orders, and second it forbids licit use of orders already held. Indirectly it also blocks a man who has become irregular from gaining a church benefice. Total irregularity bars every order and every use of orders, while partial forms bar only some. The entry sorts those kinds for readers who need the law behind a priest's fitness for office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irremovabilit:
Offices that cannot be taken away except for cause are the subject of this canon law entry, from a Latin root meaning not to be removed. Irremovability, or perpetuity, attaches to the chief church offices — pope, cardinal, bishop, parish priest — so that the holder keeps the post for life or for its set term. A pope may resign, while cardinals, bishops, and parish priests may resign or be removed only for cause.

Canonists held that a true canonical parish requires an irremovable rector. Exceptions exist, as when a rector holds only a vicar's charge for the true parish priest, and in some lands the bishop counts as parish priest of all. The entry focuses on parish priests, weighing when security of tenure protects a flock and when cause justifies removal. Readers get tenure law in miniature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kansas-city:
Kansas City was a Missouri diocese established on 10 September 1880, covering Missouri south of its great river and west of an eastern-county line, some 23,539 square miles. Suffragan of St. Louis, it began with forty-two churches, thirty priests, and twelve thousand Catholics. Its first bishop, John Joseph Hogan, transferred from St. Joseph and kept that diocese as administrator until separate jurisdiction was set up in 1893, when Maurice Burke took St. Joseph.

Hogan, born at Bruff in County Limerick in 1829, studied at the St. Louis seminary, was ordained in 1852, and was consecrated bishop in 1868 after building parishes across sparsely settled northwestern Missouri. equality:
Charles Dudley Warner opens this essay with a borrowed rule for treatises: lay down an undeniable principle first. His principle is a provocation.
